title: Stop at the first match
idea: Use break to find the first value meeting a rule and stop - the classic break use case.

exercises.explanation: The first multiple of 4 in 1..19 is 4; it prints 4 then breaks, so only 4 appears.

exercises.prompt: Why does this loop print only ONE number even though many multiples of 4 exist in the range?
exercises.explanation: break exits right after the first match, so later multiples are never reached.
options: break stops the loop after the first match

exercises.prompt: For a 'find the first ...' task, break lets you stop as soon as you succeed instead of scanning the rest.
exercises.explanation: True - that early exit is the whole point of using break here.

exercises.prompt: Arrange a loop that prints the first number over 10 in 1..20 and stops.
exercises.explanation: Loop the range, if n > 10 print it and break; the break ends the search at the first hit.
11 is the first value greater than 10, so the loop prints 11 and breaks.
break ends the loop once the first match is printed.

exercises.prompt: What prints if NO number in the range matches (e.g. looking for > 100 in 1..20)?
exercises.explanation: The if is never true, break never runs, and nothing is printed - the loop just ends normally.

exercises.prompt: With break, the order you visit values matters: you get the FIRST match in the order the loop runs.
exercises.explanation: True - break stops at the first success, so the visiting order decides which match you get.

exercises.prompt: A while version keeps asking for input until a number over 50 is entered, then breaks. Why use break?
exercises.explanation: It cleanly exits the moment the goal (a number over 50) is reached, without a separate flag.
options: It exits as soon as the goal is reached

exercises.explanation: Loop, test each value, and break on the first one that matches - then you have your answer.
options: Loop, test, break on the first match
